introduction-beyond-example-based-testin.core: Example tests only check the cases you thought of. Bugs live in the cases you didn't, so you also need generated inputs (PBT, fuzzing), well-chosen fakes and real dependencies in containers.

first_principles.problem: A function passes 2+2=4 but breaks on overflow, empty input or Unicode, none of which anyone wrote a test for.
truths: Humans pick a few inputs from an enormous space.
Edge cases cause most failures.
Fakes can drift away from reality.

analogy.title: Testing a bridge with one car
analogy.story: One car crossing proves very little; you need varied loads, wind and vibration.
analogy.breaks: More test types also mean more maintenance, so apply each where it pays.

example.title: A date parser
example.scenario: Examples miss leap years and invalid strings.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Generated inputs explore cases humans don't think of.

example.outcome: tests explore the input space rather than sample it.

check.q: What's the fundamental limit of example-based tests?
check.a: They only cover inputs the author thought of.

property-based-testing-pbt.core: Instead of fixed examples, state properties that must hold for all inputs (e.g. decode(encode(x)) == x) and let the framework generate hundreds of random cases to try to break them.

first_principles.problem: You can't hand-write enough examples to cover every list length, value and ordering.
truths: Many functions have invariants.
Machines can generate inputs cheaply.
A single counterexample disproves a property.
derivation: The framework **generates and checks** the cases.

analogy.title: Laws of physics
analogy.story: You don't drop every object to confirm gravity; you state the law and look for anything that violates it.
analogy.breaks: Writing good properties is a skill, and weak properties pass trivially.

example.title: Testing a sort

steps.label: Run
steps.detail: Hundreds of random lists, including empty ones, duplicates and negatives.

example.outcome: broad coverage from a few lines.

check.q: Give an example of a round-trip property.
check.a: parse(serialize(x)) == x for every valid x.

the-magic-of-shrinking.core: When a property fails on a huge random input, the framework shrinks it step by step to the smallest input that still fails, so you debug [0, -1] instead of 5,000 numbers.

first_principles.problem: A failing random input of 5,000 elements is almost impossible to reason about.
truths: Most bugs are triggered by a small core of the input.
Simplifying an input can be automated.
Small reproductions make bugs obvious.
derivation: Try **smaller or simpler variants** (fewer items, smaller numbers).

analogy.title: Finding which ingredient causes the allergy
analogy.story: Remove ingredients one at a time until the reaction stops. The last one removed is the culprit.
analogy.breaks: Custom generators sometimes shrink poorly unless you write shrinkers for them.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: The bug is obvious in a two-element case.

check.a: The smallest, simplest input the framework found that still makes the property fail.

fuzzing-the-bull-in-the-china-shop.core: Fuzzers throw mutated, often malformed bytes at code, guided by coverage, to find crashes, hangs and security bugs, especially in parsers and network-facing code.

first_principles.problem: Parsers trust their input, and attackers send exactly the malformed bytes nobody tested.
truths: Untrusted input is an attack surface.
Coverage feedback guides mutation toward new code paths.
Crashes and hangs signal bugs.
derivation: Write a **fuzz target** that takes bytes.
**Coverage guidance** keeps the inputs that reach new branches.

analogy.title: A bull in a china shop
analogy.story: It doesn't care how things are meant to be used; it finds every fragile shelf by smashing into it.
analogy.breaks: Fuzzers struggle with highly structured input like checksums, so use structure-aware fuzzing.

example.title: Fuzzing a config parser in Go

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: A panic on an unterminated quote, found in 30 seconds.

example.outcome: parsers stop crashing on hostile input.

check.q: How is fuzzing different from PBT?
check.a: Fuzzing mutates raw, often invalid bytes looking for crashes; PBT generates valid typed data to check properties.

faking-dependencies-the-problem.core: Unit tests should be fast, deterministic and isolated, so you replace slow or nondeterministic dependencies (APIs, databases, clocks) with controllable fakes.

first_principles.problem: A test that calls the real Stripe API is slow and flaky, costs money, and fails when the network does.
truths: External services are slow and unreliable.
Tests must give the same result every run.
You want to test your logic, not their uptime.
derivation: Replace them with **test doubles** in unit tests.

analogy.title: A flight simulator
analogy.story: Pilots practise emergencies in a simulator, not by crashing real planes.
analogy.breaks: A simulator that doesn't match the real plane trains the wrong reflexes. Fakes can drift.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Error paths become testable on demand.

check.q: Why not call real APIs in unit tests?
check.a: They are slow and flaky, cost money, and make results depend on external systems.

stubs-vs-mocks.core: A stub returns canned answers so your code can run (state verification). A mock also records how it was called so the test can assert on the interaction (behaviour verification).

first_principles.problem: Using the wrong double makes tests either too weak or brittle.
truths: Sometimes you only need input data.
Sometimes the interaction itself is the requirement.
Asserting on calls couples the test to the implementation.
derivation: Need to verify that **'X was called with Y'**? Use a **mock**.
Mock only at **real boundaries** (sending email, charging cards).

analogy.title: A cardboard cutout vs. a hidden camera
analogy.story: A cutout fills a role in the scene (stub); a hidden camera records what happened (mock).
analogy.breaks: Real-world libraries blur the terms; what matters is what the test asserts.

example.title: An order service
example.scenario: A stub for prices, a mock for the email.

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Sending the email is the requirement, so verifying the interaction is justified there.

code.text:
prices = Mock(get=lambda sku: 10)      # stub-like
mailer = Mock()
place_order("A1", prices, mailer)
mailer.send.assert_called_once()     # mock verification

example.outcome: each double has a clear purpose.

check.a: When the side effect itself is the requirement, such as an email sent or a card charged, at a system boundary.

the-danger-of-over-mocking.core: Mocking every internal call encodes the current implementation into the tests. Refactors then break tests while real bugs slip through. Test behaviour at boundaries, not wiring.

first_principles.problem: A harmless refactor breaks 40 tests that only asserted which private helpers were called.
truths: Tests should fail when behaviour breaks, not when code moves.
Mocks assert structure.
Mocked collaborators can hide integration bugs.
derivation: If setup is huge, the **design** may be the problem.

analogy.title: Rehearsing with every actor replaced by a script-reader
analogy.story: The play 'passes' rehearsal but falls apart on opening night with the real cast.
analogy.breaks: Some isolation is still needed, so the goal is balance, not zero mocks.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: Tests survive refactors and catch real regressions.

check.a: They assert implementation details, so refactors that don't change behaviour still break them.

integration-tests-in-docker.core: Spin up real dependencies (Postgres, Redis, Kafka) in throwaway containers during tests, for example with Testcontainers, so you catch problems that fakes can't model.

first_principles.problem: A mock database happily accepts invalid SQL, and the bug appears only in production.
truths: Fakes don't implement real semantics.
Containers start real software quickly and disposably.
Isolation per test run avoids shared-state flakiness.
derivation: Start the **real dependency** in a container per suite.
Keep these tests **fewer and slower** than unit tests.

analogy.title: A dress rehearsal on the real stage
analogy.story: Practise with real lights and sets before opening night, not in a classroom.
analogy.breaks: They're slower and need Docker in CI, so use them for the boundary, not every case.

example.title: Testing a repository layer

steps.label: Catch
steps.detail: A query using a non-existent column fails here, not in production.

code.text:
with PostgresContainer("postgres:16") as pg:
    engine = create_engine(pg.get_connection_url())
    run_migrations(engine)
    assert repo(engine).find_user("a@b.c") is None

example.outcome: confidence that code works with the real dependencies.

check.q: What can a container-based test catch that a mock can't?
check.a: Real SQL syntax and semantics errors, driver behaviour and migration problems.
